lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Right, let's go over the accounts, ferryman — if you don't mind — figure out exactly what you owe me, so we're not arguing about it again later.
lines.note: Brisk, professional. Hermes opens like a bookkeeper who has had this conversation before and is determined to have it properly this time.

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: Let's. Better to have it settled — less aggravation all round.
lines.note: Cooperative, but with the faint resignation of a man who already knows the total is going to be bad.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Anchor — you commissioned it, I fetched it. Five drachmas.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: By Hades himself, that's what it cost. Five drachmas. And a thole-pin: two obols.
lines.note: The oath is entirely matter-of-fact, not heated.

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: Put down five drachmas and two obols.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: And a sail-ring for the mast. I paid five obols for that.
lines.note: Continuing down the list without pause.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Wax to caulk the gaps in the hull, plus nails, plus the rope you made the sheet from — two drachmas for the lot.
lines.note: The list of small, inglorious boat-maintenance expenses is the comedy here. Deadpan delivery throughout.

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.note: The one item he can't object to, which only makes it worse.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: That's everything — unless we've missed something in the reckoning. So: when exactly are you planning to pay me back?
lines.note: Still professional. The sting is in the 'exactly.'

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: Right now? Not possible. But if a plague comes along, or a war sends a good crowd down in bulk — there's money to be made then, skimming a little off the fares.
lines.note: Entirely practical. He is not embarrassed. This is just how the cash flow works.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: So my plan is to sit here praying for catastrophe, on the off-chance I might eventually get paid?
lines.note: The line is delivered flatly. The absurdity does its own work.

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: There's no other way, Hermes. Right now, as you can see, we're getting almost nobody. It's peacetime.
lines.note: A shrug in vocal form. 'Peacetime' lands as the most forlorn possible word.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Well, peace is well enough in itself, even if it does mean you keep stringing out my debt. Though I'll tell you — the old clientele, Charon, you remember what they were like: soldiers, every one of them, soaked in blood, most of them still carrying wounds. Now it's all: poisoned by his son, or done in by his wife, or bloated from excess — swollen bellies, swollen legs — pale, the lot of them, and pathetic. Nothing like the old days. And most of them, from what I can see, ended up down here scheming over each other's money.
lines.note: The nostalgia for a more violent era of the dead is played completely straight. Hermes is not celebrating war — he is doing quality control.

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.note: Dry. One of his best lines.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Well then, I don't suppose anyone would blame me for pressing you rather hard for what you owe.
lines.note: The kicker. Returns the whole philosophical digression to the original invoice. Delivered pleasantly.
